summary: Defines an architecture and framework for a GMPLS control plane for Ethernet used as a transport network technology, in roles once held by SONET/SDH, TDM and ATM. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Ethernet is being used like a train network, and this describes how to control its tracks and switches.

subtitle: Framework for applying GMPLS routing and control to Ethernet networks used as transport networks.

tldr.problem: Ethernet was originally a local area network (LAN) technology. Modern Ethernet extensions enable it to serve as a backbone transport network (like SONET/SDH, TDM, or ATM once did), but there is no standard routed, constraint-based control plane for traffic engineering and fault recovery in these networks.
tldr.mechanism: GMPLS (Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching) is a control plane architecture that already works for optical networks, TDM, and ATM. This RFC defines how to apply GMPLS to control Ethernet, creating Ethernet Label Switched Paths (Eth-LSPs) that carry traffic along engineered routes through an Ethernet transport network.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can use a single control plane (GMPLS) to manage diverse transport technologies including Ethernet, enabling traffic engineering, automatic restoration, and integration of Ethernet with existing optical and TDM networks.

facts.label: Signaling mode options
facts.value: In-band (same links) or out-of-band (separate control network)

today: RFC 5828 is an Informational standards document that defines the framework for GMPLS control of Ethernet transport networks. It remains the architectural foundation for standards and implementations extending GMPLS to Ethernet, used by carriers deploying carrier Ethernet services with traffic engineering and high availability.

sections.title: Ethernet as a Transport Technology
sections.content:
Traditionally, Ethernet was a Local Area Network technology, connecting devices within a building or campus. Devices were connected to a spanning tree, a passive topology where only one path between any two devices was active. The path was chosen automatically by the spanning tree protocol, not by network operators.

Modern Ethernet extensions (such as Provider Backbone Bridges, or PBB, and Provider Backbone Bridges Traffic Engineering, or PBB-TE) now allow Ethernet to serve as a transport network technology, a role previously held by SONET/SDH, Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM), and Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM). In transport networks, operators need to engineer paths explicitly, manage bandwidth, provide redundancy and fast recovery, and integrate services.

However, the Ethernet extensions developed by IEEE, ITU-T, and the Metro Ethernet Forum focused on data-plane forwarding and management, but not on a routed, constraint-based control plane—the intelligence that decides which path a flow should take and manages failures. GMPLS (Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching) is exactly such a control plane. It already controls optical networks, TDM networks, and ATM networks. This RFC defines how to extend GMPLS to control Ethernet transport networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Ethernet is being upgraded from a simple local cable to a powerful long-distance transport system. This RFC explains how to control where traffic flows and what happens when something breaks.

sections.title: Ethernet Label Switched Paths (Eth-LSPs)
sections.content:
In a GMPLS-controlled Ethernet network, a label is an identifier (such as a VLAN ID or MAC address) that switches use to forward frames along a specific path. A Label Switched Path (LSP) is a predetermined path through the network where frames are forwarded using the label.

An Ethernet Label Switched Path (Eth-LSP) is an LSP over an Ethernet transport network. GMPLS creates and manages Eth-LSPs much like it manages LSPs in optical networks.

The RFC defines several types of Eth-LSPs:

  • Contiguous Eth-LSP: An end-to-end path formed from multiple Eth-LSPs, each operating within a VLAN, mapped one-to-one at VLAN boundaries.
  • Hierarchical Eth-LSP: Eth-LSPs that are nested inside other Eth-LSPs, creating a hierarchy of paths.
  • Bidirectional congruent Eth-LSP: An LSP where the forward and return paths use the same links, ports, and nodes (typical in Ethernet).
  • Point-to-point (P2P) and Point-to-multipoint (P2MP) Eth-LSPs: Paths connecting one to one endpoint, or one endpoint to many.

Ethernet forwarding can be based on VLAN ID (VID) only, or on combinations of VID and destination MAC address, or on the newer I-TAG (service instance tag). The RFC's framework accommodates all these forwarding modes.
sections.plainLanguage: An Eth-LSP is a reserved path through the Ethernet network. Think of it like a reserved lane on a highway: frames on that path get predictable treatment.

sections.title: GMPLS Control Plane for Ethernet
sections.content:
The RFC defines a GMPLS control architecture for Ethernet transport networks:

Routing: GMPLS routing protocols (such as OSPF-TE or ISIS-TE) discover the Ethernet network topology and advertise available bandwidth, VLAN availability, and other resource constraints. The routing model is adapted from GMPLS use in optical networks, reusing as much as possible.

Signaling: When an operator wants to set up an Eth-LSP, GMPLS signaling protocols (such as RSVP-TE) are used to reserve resources along the path and configure each Ethernet switch to forward frames with the chosen label along that path.

Control plane network: The control messages (routing advertisements and signaling) can be sent in-band (over dedicated VLANs on the same Ethernet links used by data) or out-of-band (over separate management links). Out-of-band signaling is more resilient because it survives data plane failures.

Link Management Protocol (LMP): GMPLS includes a protocol for discovering and managing the links between Ethernet switches, verifying that data plane and control plane connectivity are working.

Path Computation: Path computation (deciding which route an Eth-LSP should take) can use existing GMPLS algorithms. Constraints include bandwidth, VLAN availability, and end-to-end delay.
sections.plainLanguage: The control plane finds available paths, reserves bandwidth, tells switches what to do, and keeps checking that everything still works.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that deploying GMPLS control over Ethernet does not change the Ethernet data plane. All forwarding, encapsulation, and frame handling follow standard Ethernet and IEEE 802.1 rules. GMPLS only controls how switches set up and manage those paths.

Multiple VLAN service models (port-based, S-tagged, I-tagged) are supported. An operator can support multiple service types on the same network by using different GMPLS switching types, each corresponding to a forwarding model.

Different Ethernet extensions (PBB, PBB-TE, MEF services) define different forwarding models and service interfaces. The GMPLS framework accommodates them by allowing technology-specific protocol extensions in companion documents. The intent is to reuse standard GMPLS protocols where possible and add extensions only for features unique to Ethernet.

The RFC emphasizes that Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) capabilities (such as Continuity Check and Fault Fault Management defined in IEEE 802.1ag and ITU-T Y.1731) are critical for monitoring Eth-LSPs and detecting failures.
sections.plainLanguage: Eth-LSPs sit on top of normal Ethernet; switches still follow Ethernet rules, but now they follow GMPLS orders too.
